title: Against Many Worlds
abstract: Any viable interpretation of quantum theory needs to account for the Born rule, from which the theory gets its probabilistic empirical predictions. In this paper, we give an overview of possible approaches to this problem in the context of the Many Worlds interpretation. We argue that, for structural reasons, none of them can possibly succeed. More precisely, we argue that the Many Worlds interpretation must obtain the Born rule by proceeding either axiomatically, deductively, or inductively, and that all three of these approaches run into general, fundamental obstructions.
summary: This paper provides a rigorous philosophical and physical critique of how the Born rule can be justified within the Many Worlds Interpretation. The authors argue that standard logical tools—axioms, deduction, and induction—all fail to bridge the gap between unitary quantum evolution and observed probabilities. It highlights that MWI lacks an inherent mechanism to select or weight outcomes into measurable probabilities.
main_problem: The central problem is deriving the Born rule—the probabilistic link between quantum theory's unitary evolution and its empirical predictions—within the Many Worlds Interpretation (MWI). The authors argue that standard methods fail to provide this derivation.
main_result: Structurally, none of the three primary approaches (axiomatic, deductive, or inductive) can successfully account for the Born rule within MWI due to fundamental obstructions related to selection processes.
method: The paper employs a critical analysis by examining and critiquing the logical requirements of axiomatic postulation, deduction from first principles, and induction in the context of MWI's ontology.
model_or_system: The physical system is quantum theory evolving unitarily according to the Schrödinger equation. The model analyzed is the Many Worlds Interpretation (MWI), where universal wave functions decompose into non-interfering branches.
key_observables: Probabilities derived from the modulus-square of complex coefficients ($|\alpha|^2$), which must be justified as a lawlike ingredient.
important_parameters: The structure of the Hamiltonian and the nature of the wave function decomposition are central, but no specific numerical parameters are discussed.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes standard frameworks for scientific justification (axiomatic, deductive, inductive) and critiques the assumption that a physical process inherently dictates probability measures.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the problem of the Born rule in MWI by first outlining the necessity of the rule. It then dedicates sections to critiquing the axiomatic, deductive, and inductive approaches separately before concluding with a generalized statement about the difficulty of deriving probabilities.
why_interesting: While not focused on specific AMO platforms, the deep theoretical critique of probability assignment methods is highly relevant for any field dealing with open quantum systems or measurement processes where probabilistic outcomes are central.
